label: Care, Honesty and Choices (PreK to Grade 8)

lessons.title: Caring for Someone Who Is Sick
body: When someone is sick, they often feel tired, sore or sad. A kind helper can make that feel a little better. You can ask, "How are you feeling?" You can bring a blanket, draw a card, or sit quietly beside them. You can speak softly and wait while they rest.

Doctors and nurses are people whose job is caring for others. They try to help people get well, and they try to be gentle. Caring means paying attention to what the other person needs, not only what you want to do.

Here is an example. Mia's friend Sam had a tummy ache and stayed home from school. Mia could not fix the tummy ache. But she made Sam a card and told him about the funny thing that happened at recess. Sam smiled. Kind words and kind acts are real help, even when you are a kid.
If you think someone is very sick or hurt, tell a grown-up right away. That is a caring thing to do too.

lessons.title: Telling the Truth at the Doctor
body: A doctor cannot see inside your body, so the doctor asks questions. "Where does it hurt? When did it start?" The doctor needs true answers to help you. If you say your ear does not hurt when it really does, the doctor might miss the problem.

Telling the truth can feel hard if you are worried or if you think you did something wrong. Maybe you ate too many sweets and your tummy hurts. Or you forgot to wear your helmet and fell. A doctor is not there to scold you. A doctor is there to help you get better, so honest answers are the best answers.
You can also say "I don't know." That is honest too. And you can ask questions back: "What is that tool for?" Good doctors like questions.
The doctor is honest with you as well. A good doctor tells you what will happen, like "This shot will pinch for a moment." Telling the truth goes both ways, and it helps people trust each other.

lessons.title: Who Decides About Your Body?
body: Your body is yours. That is an important idea. But you are still growing, so the people who love you help you with big choices.

When you are young, your parent or caregiver usually makes health choices for you, like going to the dentist or taking medicine. Your doctor gives advice because the doctor has learned a lot about health. So the grown-ups and the doctor work together as a team, and you are on the team too.

You get to share your feelings and ask questions. A doctor may say, "I'm going to listen to your heart. Is that okay?" That is a kind way to include you. As you grow older, you will get to make more and more choices about your own body.

Some rules are always true. Nobody should touch your body in a way that makes you feel unsafe or confused. If that ever happens, say no, get away if you can, and tell a trusted grown-up. Keep telling until someone helps you. It is never your fault.

lessons.title: Being Scared and Being Brave
body: Many kids feel scared before a shot or a visit to the hospital. That is very normal. Even grown-ups feel nervous. Being scared does not mean you are weak.

Being brave does not mean feeling no fear. Being brave means you feel scared and you still do the hard thing that helps you, or you ask for help while you do it. Brave kids can say, "I'm scared." That helps the grown-ups know how to comfort you.

Here are some things that help. Take slow, deep breaths, like smelling a flower and blowing out a candle. Hold a grown-up's hand or a favorite toy. Look at a picture on the wall and count the things you see. Ask the nurse to tell you what is going to happen so there are no surprises.
After a hard thing, it is good to be proud of yourself. You did something tough, and it helped your body stay healthy.

lessons.title: What Consent Means
body: Consent means saying yes to something after you understand what it is. It has to be your own choice, not something you are pushed or tricked into. If you were not told what would happen, or you were afraid to say no, that is not real consent.

In medicine, doctors ask for permission before they do tests or treatments. For adults, the adult says yes or no. For children, the law says that a parent or guardian usually gives the permission, and the child gives what is called assent, which means agreeing and being included even though you are not the one with the legal say. A good doctor explains in words you can follow and listens to your worries.

You can also say no to touch that you do not want, even from someone you like, such as a relative who wants a hug. You can offer a high five or a wave instead. Some health care is needed to keep you safe, though, such as a shot or a stitch. In those cases a grown-up decides and the doctor tries to make it as comfortable as possible.
Asking before touching, listening to the answer and respecting it is how we show people they matter.

lessons.title: Privacy: Whose Health News Is It?
body: Privacy means some information is yours to share, or not share. Health information is a good example. Whether you have a cold, a broken arm or a sore tummy is your information. A doctor must keep your health records private and may only share them with the people who need to know in order to help you, such as your family or other doctors on your team.

Why does this matter? Imagine a classmate told everyone that you went to the hospital. You might feel embarrassed, even if there was nothing wrong with you. People tell their doctors the truth more easily when they trust that it will stay private.

There is one very important exception. A doctor, teacher or counselor must tell another grown-up if they believe someone could be in danger or being hurt. Safety comes first. That is why you should never keep a secret that makes you feel unsafe, scared or confused. Good secrets, like a surprise birthday party, are fun and end soon. Unsafe secrets should always be told to a trusted grown-up.
When a friend shares something about their health, ask yourself before you pass it on: is it mine to tell?

lessons.title: Fairness: Everyone Deserves Care
body: Fairness means treating people in a just way. In health care, many people believe that every person who needs care should be able to get it, no matter their skin color, where they were born, how much money they have, whether they have a disability, or what language they speak.

Sadly, the world is not always fair. Some towns have no clinic nearby. Some families cannot afford medicine. Some people have trouble getting care because they do not speak the same language as the doctor, so hospitals use interpreters to help.

Fairness does not always mean giving everyone the exact same thing. If two children are sick, one with a cold and one with a broken leg, it would be unfair to give both of them a tissue. Fairness means giving each person the help they need. When there is not enough of something, like a bed in the hospital, doctors have to choose carefully. They use health needs, not looks or popularity, to decide who goes first.
You can help fairness grow by including people, speaking up when someone is left out, and being kind to those who are different from you.

lessons.title: Respecting Differences
body: People are different in many ways. Some use wheelchairs, glasses, hearing aids or inhalers. Some have allergies, or learn in a different way. Some families eat special foods or have traditions about health and healing. A good health helper pays attention to these differences and respects them.

Respecting someone does not mean you have to be the same. It means you do not tease them, you do not stare, and you ask politely if you need to know something. If a classmate has diabetes and has to check their blood sugar, you can be kind and let them do it in peace. You can ask, "Is there anything I can do to help?" and then listen.

Doctors respect differences too. A doctor may ask about your family's customs, your language and what matters to you. Then the doctor tries to give care that fits you. Respect is not the same as agreeing with everything. Doctors still share what they know about safety. But they do it kindly.
A person's health condition is only one small part of who they are. They are still a friend, a classmate and a whole person.

lessons.title: How Rules Protect Patients
body: Rules in medicine can feel boring, but each one usually exists because something went wrong in the past. Doctors and nurses must be licensed, which means they have to finish training and pass exams before they treat patients. Hospitals must wash hands, label medicines and keep careful records, because tiny mistakes can harm people.

Other rules protect your choices and privacy. Patients must be told about a treatment before it is done, and hospitals must keep health records private. Medicines are tested and checked by government agencies before they are sold, so that companies cannot sell something dangerous and call it a cure.

There is also a special rule for people who study health. A researcher must get approval from a review board before doing a study with people. The board is a group that asks, "Is this safe? Is it fair? Do the people know what they are agreeing to?"

Here is a way to think about it. A seat belt can feel annoying, but it protects you in a crash. Rules in medicine are like seat belts for patients. They are not perfect, and people can argue about whether a rule is too strict or too weak, but their purpose is to keep people safe and treated with respect.

lessons.title: Why Scientists Test Things Carefully
body: Suppose a friend says, "I drank a special tea and my cold went away, so the tea cures colds!" Maybe. But colds go away by themselves in a week or so. Your friend would have felt better anyway. Scientists try not to be fooled this way, so they design fair tests.

In a clinical trial, researchers compare people who get a new treatment with people who do not. Often the groups are made by chance, which is called randomization, so that the groups are alike. Sometimes the other group gets a placebo, which is a pill or treatment with no active medicine. This is because feeling hopeful can change how you feel, so the placebo group shows how much of the improvement is from hope. In many studies, neither the patients nor the doctors know who gets which, which is called blinding. That stops people's wishes from tilting the results.

New medicines are usually tested in steps, first with small groups for safety and then with larger groups to see whether the medicine really works. Careful testing can feel slow when people are sick and waiting. But testing protects people, because some ideas that sounded great turned out to be harmful.
Testing should also be ethical. Volunteers must understand the risks, be free to stop at any time, and be treated with respect.

lessons.title: Thinking Through a Hard Choice
body: Sometimes there is no easy right answer in health care. People who study medical ethics use four helpful ideas to think a problem through. The first is respect for a person's choice, called autonomy. The second is doing good, called beneficence. The third is avoiding harm, which many people call "first, do no harm." The fourth is fairness, or justice.

Here is a story. A grandfather is very ill. The doctors say a strong treatment could help but would make him feel sick for weeks. He is not sure he wants it. His family wants him to try. What should be done?

Using the four ideas, we could ask: What does Grandpa want, and does he understand his options? That is autonomy. Could the treatment help him? That is doing good. Would it cause suffering that is worse than the benefit? That is avoiding harm. Is every option available to him, whatever his family can afford? That is fairness.

The ideas do not hand us the answer. They help us ask better questions and listen to everyone. Good thinkers do not shout. They gather the facts, hear different sides, and notice their own feelings. Sometimes thoughtful people still disagree, and that is okay when they stay respectful.

lessons.title: Your Voice and Asking for Help
body: As you move through the middle school years, your voice in your own health care grows. Doctors will explain things to you directly, ask what you think, and give you time to ask questions. For most important choices, a parent or guardian still has the legal say, but a good care team wants you to understand and to agree if you can. Your opinions are taken seriously and matter more each year.

Teens also hold some privacy. Doctors talk with you about your health, and in many places some conversations with a doctor can be private. A doctor who believes you or someone else is in danger will get help, because safety comes first.

Mental health is health. Feeling very sad, anxious or angry for a long time, or having thoughts of hurting yourself, is not a weakness or something to hide. It is a health concern, just like a broken bone or asthma, and it can be treated. If you or a friend feels this way, tell a trusted adult such as a parent, a school counselor or a doctor. In an emergency, call your local emergency number. In the United States you can also call or text 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.
Asking for help is a strong, brave and responsible choice.

questions.prompt: Sam is home with a tummy ache. Which is a caring thing a friend can do?
choices: Make him a card and tell him something funny
Tell him to hurry up and stop being sick so he can come play
Leave him alone and never ask how he is
Take his favorite toy and keep it

questions.prompt: What is the job of doctors and nurses?
choices: Helping people get well and being gentle with them
Making sure children never have any fun
Deciding which kids are the best at school
Teaching children how to ride a bike

questions.prompt: You see a classmate fall on the playground and cry a lot. What is the best thing to do?
choices: Ask the classmate to be quiet at once
Laugh and say it is nothing so the classmate stops crying
Tell a grown-up right away so they can help
Walk away and pretend you saw nothing

questions.prompt: Caring for others means paying attention to...
choices: whatever is on television that day
only the thing you personally most want to do right now
how many people are in the room
what the other person needs right now

questions.prompt: Why does the doctor ask you questions?
choices: Because questions make the visit last as long as possible
Because the doctor wants to catch you doing something bad
Because the doctor has run out of other things to say during the visit
Because the doctor cannot see inside you and needs true answers

questions.prompt: If you do not know the answer to a question, what can you say?
choices: "Yes" to every question the doctor asks
Any made-up answer at all, as long as it makes the doctor happy
"I don't know," which is an honest answer
Nothing at all and look at the floor forever

questions.prompt: Leo ate too many sweets and now has a sore tummy. What should he tell the doctor?
choices: That nothing happened and his tummy feels fine
That he ate lots of sweets, because it helps the doctor
That he cannot remember anything he ever ate
That he ate only vegetables, to avoid being in trouble

questions.prompt: A good doctor who says "This shot will pinch for a moment" is being...
choices: honest, so you know what to expect
silly, because doctors never talk about shots
rushed, because the visit is almost over
unkind, because shots should be a secret

questions.prompt: Who usually makes health choices for a young child?
choices: The child alone, with no help from anyone
A stranger who happens to be walking past the clinic door
A parent or caregiver, with advice from the doctor
The nearest friend who has the same age

questions.prompt: What should you do if someone touches you in a way that feels unsafe?
choices: Decide it was your fault and stay quiet
Wait until you are grown up to mention it
Keep it a secret so that nobody at home or school gets upset
Say no, get away if you can, and tell a trusted grown-up

questions.prompt: A doctor says, "I'm going to listen to your heart. Is that okay?" Why is that kind?
choices: It includes you and tells you what is going to happen
It means the visit is over and you can go
It means the doctor is not sure what to do and needs help
It means you must pay money for the visit

questions.prompt: As you grow older, what happens with choices about your own body?
choices: You make fewer of them than before
You get to make more of them yourself
They are made only by people far away
They stop being important to anyone

questions.prompt: What does being brave mean?
choices: Running away from every scary thing you see
Feeling scared and still doing the hard thing, or asking for help
Never feeling any fear at all, even in scary or new places
Pretending to everyone that nothing is hard

questions.prompt: Which is a way to feel calmer before a shot?
choices: Take slow deep breaths and hold a grown-up's hand
Hold your breath for as long as you possibly can until it is over
Squeeze your eyes shut and stop listening
Run out of the room and hide somewhere

questions.prompt: Ava says "I'm scared" at the clinic. What does that tell the nurse?
choices: That Ava is not a brave person
That the visit must be called off for good
That Ava should not have come at all
How to help Ava feel more comfortable

questions.prompt: Why might a nurse tell you what will happen step by step?
choices: So that the visit takes longer than it needs to
So that you cannot ask any questions at all
So there are fewer surprises and you feel safer
So you will forget about the visit completely

questions.prompt: What does consent mean?
choices: Saying yes freely after you understand what will happen
Being told what you must do by the biggest or loudest person in the room
Staying quiet because you are too scared to answer
Agreeing to something before anyone has explained it

questions.prompt: What is assent, when a child is at the doctor?
choices: The nurse picks a treatment while the family is away
The child agrees and is included, though a parent usually has the legal say
The doctor decides everything about your care and tells nobody about it
The child alone signs the papers for every treatment

questions.prompt: A relative wants a hug, but you do not feel like one. What is a respectful option?
choices: Run out of the room without saying a word
Say nothing and let them do what they want
Offer a high five or a wave instead
Hug anyway so nobody is upset with you

questions.prompt: Some health care, like a needed shot, still happens even if a child is scared. Who decides?
choices: The child, who can refuse every medical step at any age
A stranger in the waiting room who happens to have time
Nobody, because the visit is canceled whenever a child worries
A grown-up responsible for the child, with the doctor making it as comfortable as possible

questions.prompt: Whose information is your health information?
choices: It belongs to anyone who happens to be nearby at the time
It belongs to the whole class and should be announced
It belongs to nobody, so everybody can tell it
It is yours, and it should be shared only with people who need to know

questions.prompt: Which secret should you ALWAYS tell a trusted grown-up?
choices: A secret about what a gift will be on a birthday
A secret about a funny joke you plan to tell
A secret that makes you feel unsafe or scared
A secret about a surprise party you are planning for a friend

questions.prompt: Why do people tell doctors the truth more easily when records stay private?
choices: They hope the doctor will keep the secret from their family forever
They trust that the information will not be spread around
They know the doctor will tell their neighbors everything
They want the whole school to hear about the visit

questions.prompt: A classmate tells you they had to visit the hospital. What is the best thing to do?
choices: Ask if they want to talk about it, and keep it private unless they say otherwise
Tell all your other friends right away so everyone knows what happened
Post a photo of the classmate in the hospital so people can see
Make jokes about the visit so the classmate will laugh at it too

questions.prompt: What does fairness in health care mean?
choices: People who look the same as the doctor should always go first
Care should only be given to the people who live closest by
Each person who needs care should be able to get it, no matter who they are
People who own the most toys or games should always be seen first by the doctor

questions.prompt: Why do some hospitals use interpreters?
choices: To make the visits much shorter so that the doctor can go home earlier in the day
To teach children how to draw pictures of their bodies
To decide who will be seen first in the waiting room
To help patients and doctors understand each other when they speak different languages

questions.prompt: One child has a cold and another has a broken leg. Which is the fair way to help?
choices: Give each child the help that fits what they need
Give both children the same tissue and send them home
Help whichever child is more popular at school first
Help neither child until both of them have stopped crying

questions.prompt: When a hospital has only one bed left, how should doctors choose who gets it?
choices: By offering it to the person who arrived at the hospital last
By how urgently each person needs it for their health
By picking the person with the nicest clothes or the most friends
By choosing the person who asks the loudest in the hallway

questions.prompt: What does it mean to respect differences?
choices: Asking people loud questions about their body in front of others
Not teasing or staring, and being kind to people who are not the same as you
Pretending that everyone is exactly the same as you in every possible way
Staying far away from classmates who use glasses, hearing aids or inhalers

questions.prompt: Which is a kind way to help a classmate who needs to check their blood sugar?
choices: Let them do it in peace and ask if they would like any help
Watch closely and tell everyone what they are doing
Ask them again and again why they have to do it
Tease them so the moment feels less serious

questions.prompt: A doctor asks about your family's customs. Why might the doctor do that?
choices: To write down a list of health rules that every family must follow
To find out which families are better than other families
To fill the time until the next patient comes in
To give care that fits what matters to you and your family

questions.prompt: A person's health condition is...
choices: something that makes them less of a person
a reason to treat them as a stranger at school
only one small part of who they are
the only important thing to know about them

questions.prompt: Why must doctors and nurses be licensed?
choices: They must complete training and pass exams before treating patients
Licenses let them skip hand washing and other safety rules on busy days
Licenses allow them to skip keeping any records on patients
They are only needed so that hospitals can charge higher prices

questions.prompt: What is the job of a research review board?
choices: To tell researchers which volunteers must stay in the study
To ask whether a study is safe, fair and clearly explained to participants
To pick the studies that will make the most money for a company that pays for them
To make sure that no study ever finds any new information

questions.prompt: Why are medicines checked by government agencies before they are sold?
choices: So that every medicine is guaranteed to work for each person
So that doctors never need to explain medicine to anyone
So companies cannot sell something dangerous and call it a cure
So that all medicines cost exactly the same amount in every store in the country

questions.prompt: The lesson compares medical rules to seat belts. What is the point of the comparison?
choices: They are always perfect, so no one ever needs to question them
They are only for people who have already been in an accident
They exist so that people will not want to go to a hospital
They can feel annoying, but they protect people when something goes wrong

questions.prompt: In a clinical trial, what is a placebo?
choices: A machine that scans the inside of the body for a doctor
A type of vaccine that is made only for young children
A treatment with no active medicine, used to compare with a real one
A very strong medicine that is given only to the sickest people in the hospital

questions.prompt: What is randomization in a clinical trial?
choices: Letting each volunteer choose the group they believe will help them the most
Putting only the healthiest people in the group with the new treatment
Changing the groups halfway through the study to see what happens
Using chance to decide who goes into which group so the groups are alike

questions.prompt: Your friend drank tea and her cold went away, so she says the tea cures colds. What is the main problem with that claim?
choices: Colds often get better on their own, so the tea may not have done anything
Tea is always dangerous, so nobody should ever drink it while they are ill
Colds cannot ever go away without a doctor giving medicine
Only scientists are allowed to drink tea when they are sick

questions.prompt: Why do scientists test new medicines in steps, starting small?
choices: To make it impossible for the results to ever be checked again
To check safety first before giving it to larger groups of people
To make sure that the finished medicine ends up as expensive as it can be
To keep the medicine hidden from the volunteers who are in it

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the four ideas used to think about medical ethics?
choices: Respect for a person's own choice
Avoiding harm to the patient
Fairness in how people are treated
Making the most money for the hospital

questions.prompt: What does autonomy mean?
choices: A rule that says that all people must get the same treatment
A way to avoid talking about difficult health choices
A person's right to make choices about their own care
The idea that doctors always know best about every choice a patient faces

questions.prompt: In the story, Grandpa is unsure about a strong treatment. Which question is about avoiding harm?
choices: Is every option open to him no matter what his family can pay?
Would the treatment cause suffering that is worse than its benefit?
What does Grandpa actually want, and does he understand the options?
Could the treatment possibly help him feel better in the future?

questions.prompt: Two thoughtful people still disagree about a hard health question. What does the lesson say is okay?
choices: Disagreeing while staying respectful and listening to each other
Shouting louder and louder until the other person finally agrees with you
Pretending to agree so the whole conversation can end quickly
Refusing to listen to anyone who has a different opinion

questions.prompt: As teens get older, what usually happens with their voice in health care?
choices: It grows, and doctors explain things to them directly and ask what they think
It disappears, and teens are no longer told anything about their own care
It stays exactly the same until the day they turn eighteen
It is replaced by the voices of whoever is in the waiting room

questions.prompt: Which statement about mental health is the most accurate?
choices: a topic that doctors are not allowed to talk about at all
part of health, and problems can be treated like other health problems
a sign of weakness that people should always hide from friends and family
only a concern for adults and never for children or teens

questions.prompt: A friend tells you they have thought about hurting themselves and asks you to keep it secret. What should you do?
choices: Post about it online so that lots of people can offer advice
Tell your friend to stop feeling that way and change the subject
Tell a trusted adult right away, because safety comes before the secret
Keep the secret and simply hope that your friend will feel better soon on their own

questions.prompt: Why might a doctor break privacy and get other people involved?
choices: Because the doctor finds the story interesting and wants to share it with colleagues
Because the patient has asked them a lot of questions at the visit
Because privacy rules only apply during the first five minutes
Because they believe someone is in danger and safety comes first
